did_you_know.text: Did you know? Isaiah’s prophecy describes the LORD coming against Egypt "riding on a swift cloud," and as he appears, the idols of Egypt tremble and the heart of Egypt melts.
Did you know? Egypt’s crisis is described as civil war and internal division: everyone against his brother, city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.
Did you know? When Egypt’s counsel fails, its people turn not only to idols but also to mediums, spiritists, and diviners—practitioners of divination and sorcery mentioned in the verse.
Did you know? The calamity in Egypt includes damage to its water sources: the waters fail, the river becomes dry and parched, and the canals dwindle.
Did you know? The drying up of the Nile directly harms the fishing industry: the fishermen mourn, those who cast their hooks grieve, and those who spread their nets languish.
Did you know? Isaiah portrays the officials of Zoan and the wise counselors of Pharaoh as foolish in their counsel, questioning their claim to be descendants of the wise and of ancient kings.

Did you know? Alongside the description of calamity, the chapter describes a spiritual change in Egypt: five cities in the land of Egypt will speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of hosts; one of them will be called "City of Destruction."
Did you know? According to the chapter, there will be an altar to the LORD in the middle of Egypt and a pillar near its border, as a sign and witness to the LORD of hosts.
Did you know? The chapter’s vision describes a highway between Egypt and Assyria, with Egypt and Assyria maintaining mutual contact; thus regional enemies become part of a new reality.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, Egypt and Assyria are no longer presented merely as enemy nations: the LORD calls Egypt "my people," Assyria "the work of my hands," and Israel "my inheritance," and blesses all three.
